newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh tribal repatriation to resume shortly.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh tribal repatriation to resume shortly.

text.p: Repatriation of some 43,000 tribal refugees who fled to northeast India to escape a separatist insurgency in Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts will resume shortly, officials said on Saturday.

"We are hoping to resume the repatriation soon as refugee leaders and Indian officials now visiting the Hill Tracts said they are satisfied with the rehabilitation process," one Hill Tract official said.
Nearly 7,000 refugees -- all tribespeople -- returned to the area in southeast Bangladesh in the first phase of repatriation in March-April.
Both sides then agreed that the next phase would begin after a survey by refugee leaders and officials of India's northeastern Tripura state which sheltered the tribespeople for 10 years or more.
A 14-member team including three Tripura officials arrived on Thursday and met those who returned in the first phase.

"We expect the next phase will begin soon as most of the first phase returnees have been rehabilitated according to the government's pledges," Tripura official Lok Ranjan told Hill Tracts officials at Khagrachhari hill town on Friday night.
"This time the (Bangladesh) government has proved its sincerity...so all of the remaining refugees would prefer to return home," refugee leader Ranjit Narayan Tripura told reporters on Saturday.
On their return each refugee family received 15,000 taka ($344), free food rations for a week, house-building materials and money to buy livestock, officials said.
Before returning to Tripura on Saturday evening the team is to visit severel more villages where refugees have been resettled, officials said.
"I hope they will go back fully impressed that everything here has been going on smoothly," one Bangladesh official told reporters.

The tribal influx to Tripura was triggered by a long-running insurgency by tribal Shanti Bahini guerrillas over demands for autonomy for the 5,500 sq-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma.
They also want some 500,000 Bengali-speaking settlers to be expelled from the vast region, which they consider a tribal homeland.
More than 8,500 people, including rebels, security personnel and civilian, have been killed in the insurgency, according to official figures.
While persuading the refugees to come back the Bangladesh government also held peace talks with the political wing of the Shanti Bahini, the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Sanghati Samity (PCJSS).
Officials said broad outlines of a peace agreement between the government and the PCJSS had already been reached and the deal was expected to be formally initialled in the second half of June.
They said the insurgency since 1973 had delayed development activities in the Hill Tracts and fuelled rivalries between tribespeople and settlers, who often fought savage battles.
"The innocent tribespeople were held virtually hostage by the guerrillas, who tortured them for money, support and shelter," one tribal village headman said on Saturday.
"We only wish for an end to the unnecessary blood-letting and acrimony," he said.
